An unobserved decay of $B^0_s$ meson into two kaons, $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$, is being used to create a method for detecting the CP-violating phase in the standard model. To achieve this goal, it is crucial to determine the decay length of this process, $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$, with a high level of precision. 

In this research, the current understanding of this quantity's precision and systematics is evaluated, based on around $103\mu b$ $pp$ collision data collected by the LHCb experiment during proton-proton collisions at 7 and 8 TeV energy levels.

A refined strategy for improving precision in the determination of the decay length is proposed, along with projected outcomes that could reach a precision of 0.12 picoseconds by the end of 2015, which would significantly fall short of required standards. 

In addition, the significance of employing $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays as a function of two variables, combining the decay length and CP asymmetry, is highlighted for the first time. 

The research demonstrates that achieving the necessary precision in the determination of the decay length is challenging with existing LHCb data, which necessitates either a substantial increase in data volume or the development of alternative methods.

This paper introduces a numerical method for a class of distributed control systems modeled by a stochastic evolution equation, specifically a parabolic equation with significant diffusion and control affecting a part of the spatial domain. We demonstrate that under appropriate conditions, this method converges to an optimal solution for a time-invariant control problem. To achieve this, we first show that a discrete version of the continuous problem exists and is unique. Next, we establish the required monotonicity and boundedness conditions necessary for convergence. Finally, we present numerical results illustrating the approach.

A study by the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant fluctuations in ultra-high energy cosmic rays at energies exceeding 4 EeV, with variations of up to 10 times the predicted standard deviation when looking at groups of 12 nearby arrivals. These fluctuations among cosmic rays with energies between 4.5 EeV and 100 EeV are consistent with a source distribution that is evenly spread across the sky, with no predominant angles observed. It is also found that heavier cosmic rays exhibit larger-scale fluctuations among their more massive counterparts. The findings imply that cosmic rays with energies up to 100 EeV are composed of numerous, distinct, high-energy sources, with significantly varying power outputs, rather than a single homogeneous source, such as an active galactic nucleus powered by a supermassive black hole.

The ATLAS particle detector at the Large Hadron Collider's energy source, LHC, was utilized to analyze proton-proton and lead-proton collisions at high energy levels. By examining detected particles moving at various speeds, researchers re-created proton-proton reference data and calculated nuclear alteration factors for lead-proton collisions. These calculations revealed that particles produced in lead-proton collisions are significantly altered when compared to proton-proton collisions, with alterations depending on particle properties such as mass and electric charge. Additionally, predictions for lead-proton collisions based on proton-proton data and nuclear alteration factors showed good agreement with actual detected particle data, further validating their use as a reliable tool.

This study explores the fundamentals of quantum mechanics within a noncommutative geometric framework, focusing on the potential applications of Lie algebras in this context. We begin by establishing the principles of noncommutative quantum mechanics, moving on to examine specific algebraic structures, including the deformation of Heisenberg algebras, Weyl algebras, and Poisson algebras, all of which are centrally motivated. We then investigate the implications of these structures for physical observations, discussing the role of noncommutative geometry in quantum field theories. Some preliminary findings on subalgebras, deformed Hamiltonians, and monogenic theories are presented, highlighting the benefits of this approach, before concluding with an overview of the key challenges and an examination of potential links to established theories, such as Yang-Mills quantum mechanics.

In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to classify tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL) categories, a critical aspect in cancer treatment and research. Due to the presence of sensitive medical data, an added layer of security is necessary, which federated learning provides by enabling training without exchanging data. We compared the results of training models on both federated and centralized platforms, finding that federated learning yields comparable accuracy while ensuring the protection of confidential medical information. This success paves the way for adopting federated learning in other sensitive data scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/ghammam/til-quantification-FL.

In this study, a high-speed fiber transmission system is demonstrated, reaching data rates of 72Gbit/s per wavelength in a 480km undersea cable installation. However, the system is prone to frequent high-speed bursts due to nonlinear interference, severely hindering equalization. To address this challenge, a decision-feedback equalizer was integrated with a novel burst-error propagation mitigation technique, effectively suppressing the non-linear effects and maintaining a 9Gbit/s margin at the equalizer output. As a result, a 56Gbit/s QAM transmission system was successfully deployed in a real underwater fiber transmission environment, showcasing a 20% increase in data transfer rate compared to existing 4QAM technology.

Temporal convolutional networks have gained popularity in various tasks due to their flexible and real-time capability to process time-series data of any length. However, their potential is hindered by inefficient network scaling, limited feature learning across time, and persistent issues with causal convolution computation. Current optimization strategies for TCNs, such as dynamic trimming and learning temporal distillation, are often complicated and unsuitable for real-time applications. In our research, we present a straightforward trimming-in-time (PIT) method that simultaneously addresses over-scaling, poor feature learning, and inefficient convolution computation. PIT involves trimming the network in both spatial and temporal dimensions, as well as the introduction of a temporal fence to modulate the learning of network inputs. By leveraging a dual pathway structure, our method enhances cross-time feature learning and facilitates efficient causal convolution computation. We evaluate PIT on several real-time TCN applications and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving accuracy while maintaining low latency.
This paper proves that any variety of linear algebras, which includes but is not limited to, nilpotent, solvable, and abelian algebras, necessarily encompasses all Zinbiel algebras.

This study provides first-time data on the fluctuation of stream detection angle and flow intensity in Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV. Based on ALICE detector data, the dependence of stream detection angle fluctuations on flow intensity is documented, demonstrating a notable change from negative to positive fluctuations when moving from lower-intensity flows to higher-intensity flows, which aligns with theoretical predictions. Additionally, the dependence of flow-intensity fluctuations on stream detection angle was found, showing an increase in fluctuations when detecting streams at more forward angles, which could offer insights into initial conditions and the collective behavior of matter in the ALICE detector.

The concept of correspondence theory for dynamic logic with propositional modalities was introduced, covering varieties like S5, CP, and BP. Correspondence can be expressed through both forward and reverse approaches. While the forward method is integral to the theory, the reverse approach has received limited attention. In this research, a comprehensive framework for dynamic logic with correspondence relations and propositional modalities is presented, with a focus on the reverse approach. We leverage this framework to derive results for specific logics, such as CP, BP, and their modal dynamic counterparts, using a unified strategy. Moreover, our work enables the identification of satisfying worlds for a given formula within the context of DLE-Logics.

Information studios aim to provide users with personalized views of consolidated datasets. These views are generated from merged tables, which themselves are derived from multiple underlying data sources. To achieve this, information studios employ a technique called two-tier table summarization. This process involves two stages: first, combining the input tables, possibly including handling for missing values and inherent data constraints; second, computing a summary of the combined table. Focusing on the initial stage, this work invests in developing methods to manage discrepancies among the input tables. Specifically, it explores ways to handle missing data and underlying data constraints known as functional dependencies within the combined table. Notably, this research recognizes the challenge of identifying functional dependencies as unsolved, whereas discovering and utilizing missing data is viewed as a solvable problem. As a result, this work concentrates on the second stage of two-tier summarization, incorporating missing data and FDs into the computation of the summary. Finally, it proposes a dependency-preserving aggregation function, applicable when the data sources contain no discrepancies.

This study presents a novel mathematical approach to modeling time-varying Poisson autoregressive processes. Our model maintains the characteristics of traditional PAR processes while adapting to changing time series patterns. Notably, our model offers a flexible framework that accommodates both constant and time-varying coefficients, seamlessly bridging the gap between time-dependent PAR and general time-series models. We have successfully demonstrated that our model produces statistically meaningful forecasts and reduces prediction error when compared to conventional time-series methods. Additionally, we have established a method for estimating model parameters and provided a framework for assessing model fitness. Finally, we illustrate the applicability of our model by analyzing real-world data sets.

In robotics, using neural networks for object recognition and manipulation has seen growing interest due to their potential to handle a wide range of tasks and adaptability to various environments. However, employing neural networks for task-specific manipulation requires object descriptors that remain consistent across different positions, orientations, and lighting conditions. Object descriptors that are not invariant to these variations may cause the network to learn extraneous tasks, focusing on the underlying features rather than the object itself. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes neural networks to create descriptor fields, enabling the representation of objects in a way that is SE(3)-invariant. This approach allows for the recognition of objects in different states and enables their direct use in manipulation tasks. In experiments, we demonstrated that objects can be identified, separated from others, and picked up using a gripper based on their SE(3)-invariant descriptors. Additionally, compared to descriptors that are only invariant to changes in rotation and lighting, those that are fully SE(3)-invariant provide a level of performance in manipulation tasks.

The SiD (Scinning Detector) concept has been a leading proposal for the future large scale colliders such as the ILC (International Linear Collider).  With momentum carried from the past, the SiD detector remains one of the leading options for the future linear e+e- colliders.  Although initially designed for the ILCSiD, its outstanding performance makes it a suitable detector also for the future circular e+e- colliders like the Future e+e- linear collider and FCCee.  This contribution will present the recent R&D and revision made on the SiD sensor concept,  focusing on the development of the silicon sensor detector components,  discussing possible revised design that maintain or improve performance while reducing cost,  and illustrating the working prototype of the SiD CALIBRATION system.

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, significantly above average levels for this region, suggesting a multi-generational population within the cluster that consists of first-generation nitrogen-abundance members. A [Ce/Fe] spread was identified and found to correlate with nitrogen, suggesting a relatively minor, s-process enriched population within the cluster which was probably the result of smaller low-mass Asymptotic Giant Branch stars. A radial velocity mean of -178.6 km/s and minimal velocity dispersion of 2.99 km/s was discovered for the cluster, indicative of typical globular cluster features, including an eccentric orbit.

The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, offering an extensive range of research opportunities for students to engage in project work. Despite this, there exist few documented cases of successful project verification projects using FPs in Isabelle. This issue persists due to the complex and time-consuming nature of understanding Isabelle'sore (e-theses) proofs, often requiring multiple weeks or even months of effort from students. As a result, students may become disheartened and lose interest in theorem verification projects. In contrast, theorem verification projects using Isabelle's pure (p-theses) proofs are more accessible and can be completed within a shorter timeframe. To address the existing limitations of FP projects, this project first conducted a comprehensive analysis of FP proofs in Isabelle, focusing on areas such as proof structure, complexity, required student skills, and potential areas of expansion for the Isabelle community. Secondly, this project aims to create a clear, step-by-step guide for students to follow when working on Isabelle FP project verification projects. Lastly, to enhance the FP project collection in Isabelle, this project will develop a new verification project based on a previously unaddressed theorem from the "Algebra" section of the Isabelle Library.

In statistical mechanics, the Yang-Lee edge singularity represents a phase transition between pairs of classical field theories that share a symmetry. We have mathematically proven that this edge singularity occurs at a specific critical point for all universality classes that involve a high degree of symmetry, specifically O(N) symmetries, where N is ten or greater.

In statistical mechanics, the Thermodynamic Average with the use of the pseudo-inverse minimization method, known as TAP, establishes a self-consistent set of equations to determine the system's free energy and thermodynamic properties. However, the local concavity of the TAP free energy is a crucial assumption in the Generalized TAP equation can sometimes fail to yield a valid solution. Through the application of the Fourier-Motzkin elimination method, we demonstrate that the TAP free energy exhibits local concavity within a specific region of the parameter space. Moreover, we derive an explicit condition for the stability of the TAP equation and demonstrate that the quasi-Dreamland region of the spin variables correlates directly with the asymptotic regime of the generalized TAP equation. Using the Bubnov-Skobey theorem, we prove the existence of a solution to the generalized TAP equation under specific conditions.

Recent advancements in radio frequency metamaterials, specifically those comprising flat, two-dimensional units, has led to significant breakthroughs, particularly in the development of tunable devices. Unfortunately, the field of microwave metamaterials lacks an established computational framework that accurately models two-dimensional radio frequency metamaterials, which is crucial for designing and optimizing these devices. Currently, available methods face critical limitations, including but not limited to, difficulty in capturing electromagnetic interaction between neighboring units, a lack of rigorous electric field excitation, and inadequate characterization of frequency-dependent responses. As a result, there is a pressing need to develop a reliable and versatile numerical approach that tackles these challenges and provides a robust foundation for the computational analysis of two-dimensional radio frequency metamaterials. As part of this study, we propose a novel method that leverages high-frequency structural simulation tools and electromagnetic volume integral equations to create a unified framework for modeling these metamaterials under plane-wave excitation. This method boasts enhanced computational accuracy, capturing electromagnetic unit interactions and other key phenomena, and has been successfully validated through a series of numerical tests and experiments. As a result, this new approach has the potential to accelerate the design of two-dimensional radio frequency metamaterials and even facilitate the development of complex, three-dimensional structures through tissue slabs.

The primary objective of this research is to validate the smooth local orbital linearization theorem for vector fields in any dimension, assuming only that they have a nontrivial invariant distribution that includes the vector field itself. Our proof employs a combination of techniques, drawing from the works of Sternberg and Thurston, along with local and global approaches, building upon previous contributions from the second author and his collaborators.

Accurate descriptions of electron interactions, as seen in the full configuration interaction (FCI) solution, are crucial for a thorough understanding of multi-electron systems. However, as the number of electrons and orbitals increases, FCI calculations become impractically demanding, rendering existing methods ineffective. In this study, a deep learning approach, Configuration Interaction Electron Recurrent (CI-Rec), is introduced to efficiently capture the intricate electron interactions common in 2nd row d-shell atoms by transcending existing many-body perturbation theory limitations. CI-Rec achieves remarkable results for 18 electrons across 6 different atoms (boron through sulfur) when compared to FCI standards, exceeding existing methods in precision and universality. Additionally, CI-Rec makes it possible to derive reliable effective single-particle descriptions, facilitating the use of this model in applications where these descriptions are crucial.

We have discovered a massive curved structure in the cosmic web at z=0.027, comprising over 20 million galaxies within a 1.3 billion h^-1^- kpc arc. Spanning approximately 260 h^-1^- kpc in radius, this feature is distinguished from nearby cosmic web branches due to its unique spectral properties, as revealed through the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and EGADS. The curved arc is comprised of galaxy distributions that form an almost complete circle, with about 10% of its galaxies residing in notable galaxy clusters. We propose that this feature is a massive curved wall, a phenomenon that can be explained through the gravitational interaction of two pairs of galaxy clusters moving at high speeds in the plane of the web.

The use of photometry from space-based telescopes offers a new approach to measuring the altitude of aerosol layers in the atmosphere. This methodology uses the scattering of starlight by multiple layers of aerosols in the atmosphere to derive their individual heights. Recent advancements in this field involve the application of new mathematical models to accurately describe the scattering of light, which has led to a significant reduction in associated errors. By utilizing this method and data from the Kepler space telescope, a new technique has been developed to measure the altitude of aerosol layers with an average error of 194.8 meters, alongside other parameters including angular thickness and surface density.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using deep learning methods has gained significant interest. These approaches, particularly those based on matching images to pre-captured datasets, have achieved high accuracy but are hampered by slow performance and limited robustness due to sequential pose estimation and lack of integrated correspondence checking. To address these issues, we present a novel, end-to-end framework called DeepHMap++, which simultaneously learns pose estimation and correspondence by grouping 2D projection points into matching pairs. This multi-task design leverages a correspondence checking network to improve pose estimation accuracy and a pose estimation network to refine correspondence. Through batch normalization modification and gradient masking, DeepHMap++ overcomes the pose estimation bias. Extensive experiments on the LPD Dataset and CMU Pose, Pack, and Grab Dataset demonstrate that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art in pose estimation accuracy, scale consistency, and correspondence rate.

Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in their application across multiple disciplines, offering a unique and innovative approach to studying complex problems. This review focuses on the bond-based peridynamic model, examining its potential to model nonlocal phenomena in fluid mechanics. By enhancing the traditional continuum mechanics framework with bond-based PD, researchers can capture internal failures and material degradation within fluids, as well as other material properties that cannot be modeled using local theories. The review explores the mathematical formulation of the bond-based peridynamic model, discussing its potential to describe fluid mechanics phenomena through nonlocal stress and strain measures. It also highlights the model's potential to be formulated using different types of material functions and strain energy function approaches. Furthermore, this review provides numerical methods for solving PD equations, including mesh-free methods, and applies the bond-based PD model to solve various problems, such as static and dynamic fracture in solids and quasi-static and dynamic fluid-fluid, fluid-solid interactions, before examining its implications for bridge damage detection using machine learning and image processing.

We present GGLasso, a Python-based library that offers an user-friendly interface for users to access and manipulate complex matrices associated with Sparse Estimation problems, including Generalized Graphical Lasso, Lasso, and Group Lasso, among others. Additionally, GGLasso provides a straightforward way for users to addological constraints to their matrix variables, reducing the need for unnecessary data storage. By leveraging the Cython and C++ back-end, GGLasso achieves competitive performance in computing time for several sparse estimation techniques, such as GLasso, Lasso and Group Lasso, especially when dealing with larger datasets.

Our study highlights the advantages of using Langevin dynamics with high temperature fluctuations to rapidly explore complex molecular configurations, leveraging numerical simulations to illustrate these benefits. By simplifying the energy landscape with a high temperature, we significantly reduce configurational barriers that hinder molecular movement. We discovered that through the damping parameter and temperature relationship ($\xi TL = k_B$, where $\xi$ is the friction coefficient and $L$ the system length), we can effectively mitigate oscillatory behavior when combining molecular dynamics with mesoscale simulations. We propose modifying the transition state theory to account for temperature-dependent fluctuations, which provides a precise framework for identifying rate-determining steps in molecular reactions. Finally, we demonstrated that temperature-dependent fluctuations in molecular dynamics can be accurately captured using a much shorter simulation time, thereby substantially increasing simulation efficiency.

We utilized highly sophisticated computer programs to model the collision of two rotating black holes in various environments, including those with a type of dark energy that affects gravitational waves. Unlike previous similar simulations, we used a different computer program to model the dark energy, which produced minor variations in the results. We found that these variations have a clear pattern and are largely consistent with the limitations of the original computer program used. Furthermore, we found that the computer programs used to model the collision of the black holes were consistent with each other, particularly in the cases where the same type of dark energy was modeled.
We have established a priori stability for small, elongated Euler-Bernoulli beams on star-shaped graphs near equilibria where the beam is symmetric and perpendicular to its long axis.

This novel acoustic lens material possesses a wider detection range, extending from very low frequency wavelengths associated with thick breast tissue to high frequency wavelengths indicative of solid tissues like muscle and bone. 

To illustrate this feature's effectiveness, a numerical simulation was conducted under both ideal and practical conditions. The results showed that the new acoustic lens material doubles the detection region compared to traditional polymers, such as PMMA. 

Additionally, experiments using two different detectors, one ideal and one prone to signal attenuation, demonstrated detection capabilities down to 200 MHz. Notably, this detection range is significantly better than the 50 MHz achieved with PMMA.

Our research focuses on a significant issue in multilayer network analysis, where the concept of node significance varies depending on the layer. In contrast to traditional approaches that apply the same importance assessment to different layers, we're working with networks where the significance of nodes is defined differently across each layer. This distinction brings a new level of complexity to the evaluation of node importance, particularly when considering that nodes with high connectivity in some layers may have low connectivity in others. To address this challenge, we're proposing a new method to quantify the prominence of nodes in multilayer networks. This method involves a composite index that combines the significance of nodes in each layer, along with a new metric to account for the reliability of layers. To calculate the prominence of nodes, we use a variant of the eigenvector method that takes into account the dependable connectivity of nodes across all layers. This approach ensures that nodes with high connectivity in layers with strong connections are considered more significant than those with high connectivity in layers that are less reliable. Finally, we apply our proposed method to real-world datasets, including scientific collaborations and international air traffic, and demonstrate its effectiveness by comparing the results with existing methods.

We tackle the issue of non-blind demosaicking and denoising raw images in a new way by treating demosaicking as a crucial preprocessing step that provides valuable information to both denoising and deblurring processes. We utilize a joint model that combines demosaicking, deblurring, and denoising by incorporating the demosaicking process as a feature extraction component, extracting information that is then utilized by a collaborative deblurring and denoising network. To train this joint model, we make use of the demosaicked images produced during training, mimicking real-world processing pipelines. Experiments show that our method yields superior outcomes when compared to standard demosaicking followed by deblurring and denoising, particularly noticeable in situations with low light levels. Code is readily available for download at https://github.com/ghiyam/GDnD.

In $R$-Minkowski spacetime, the metric tensor is adjusted by a scalar function $f$, leading to a modified Dirac equation that incorporates the gravitational field. This study examines the equation in question and establishes its relationship to the conventional Dirac equation. It is demonstrated that the conventional equation results when the variation of the gravitational field is negligible. Furthermore, we derive an approximate solution to the modified equation, utilizing a variational approach that treats the gravitational field as a perturbation. This outcome shows that the conventional Dirac equation and its solutions remain coherent when the gravitational field is minimal; however, the presence of significant gravitational effects leads to a departure from this consistency.

Introducing the Causal Exploration Toolbox (CET), a free and open-source software for Python that facilitates the discovery of causal relationships in various data settings. CET automates the creation of interventions and the subsequent data collection for both real and simulated interactive environments. It seamlessly integrates with established causal inference tools and utilities, while also providing access to well-known datasets and virtual environments for testing and validation. With its user-friendly interface, users can easily explore and identify causal connections within the data by executing intuitive commands. Furthermore, CET is highly adaptable, as it permits the incorporation of custom models and the definition of tailored learning objectives, making it an invaluable resource for users seeking to uncover causal relationships in data.

Our research focused on the seal mechanism of spheres in liquid environments at medium to high speeds. Contrary to commonly held beliefs, our findings suggest that the "liquid entry surface seal" phenomenon is not solely responsible for preventing gas escape when spheres move through liquids at these speeds. Instead, we discovered that this seal mechanism is incomplete, allowing gas to leak out. As a result, we propose that the "surface seal" and "base seal" work together to minimize gas release when spheres move through liquids. Based on our findings, we developed a theoretical model to explain this seal mechanism when spheres move through liquids at medium to high speeds, challenging the existing paradigm held by the "liquid entry surface seal" theory.

We investigate a class of Type IIB NUT charges that are irrelevant at the effective field theory level, specifically those related to three-leg vertices involving the graviphoton and two gauginos. Our analysis reveals that these charges can break a global $SU(4)$ symmetry present in four-dimensional supergravity, potentially introducing a non-trivial phase factor in the three-leg vertex interactions. This potential phase shift can be viewed as an extended theta-term in the effective theory. We demonstrate that this charge is conserved across a particular path in the field theory's configuration space, which we identify as the 'B-type' slice. This conservation implies that the phase factor remains constant within this specific subset of the theory's parameter space. We further establish that the charge can differentiate the vacuum energy levels of the effective theory, leading to a non-trivial dependence of the B-type conservation law on the theta angle. Finally, we consider the implications of these findings for the effective theory's realisation of the AdS$_3$ algebra, and the associated chiral supermultiplets that arise in four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=4$ supergravity constructed from NUT charges.

In order to reduce the risk of sophisticated software-based attacks, the latest generation of high-end computing platforms, such as Apple M1 and various Windows laptops, incorporate hardware isolation capabilities. However, the isolated hardware segments pose a significant performance challenge, as demonstrated by the limited processing power and memory size of the Windows Hello face authentication process. This research focuses on optimizing the performance of Windows Hello by prioritizing the reduction of confidence levels required for authentication, rather than achieving the fastest possible results. By conducting extensive experiments on various hardware configurations, we have identified that a lower confidence level can often be achieved with isolated hardware at a fraction of the time it takes to reach the maximum level, indicating that Windows Hello can be successfully authenticated with a lower threshold in a shorter isolated hardware time period. By applying this finding to real-world scenarios, we have developed an innovative approach to utilize isolated hardware more efficiently. As a result, we have created a new Windows Hello configuration that achieves a 5 times faster time-to-acceptable-level and 30% less time-to-acceptance compared to the original setting, without sacrificing system security.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly used in critical systems like self-driving cars and medical diagnosis, often dealing with significant data losses due to sensor failure, misdiagnosis, or other severe corruption. Although value-based methods can tolerate some level of corruption, they are not designed to handle the full extent of RL data losses. In contrast, policy gradient (PG) methods are highly effective in exploring state spaces efficiently, but they struggle with significant data corruption, or "bypassing," where they get stuck in a local minimum. This challenge forces PG to rely heavily on the initial exploration data, limiting its potential. This paper introduces a novel RL algorithm called Robust Policy Gradient (RPG), which enhances the stability of PG by incorporating a robust objective function that resists severe data corruption. Through theoretical analysis and extensive experiments on various environments, including those with controlled and extreme data corruption, RPG consistently outperforms the baseline PG method. Notably, in scenarios with significant corruption, RPG achieves a 5-10 times improvement in reward return. This suggests that RPG can handle critical applications more effectively, or in scenarios where severe data corruption is inevitable, or in settings where training data has a high entropy.

In our proposed model, agents make choices independently, without influence or communication, yet our mathematical proofs reveal a persistent issue with fastest completion time in the box game for all agent types. Additionally, this problem persists as the number of agents increases infinitely, presenting a challenging problem in combinatorial optimization.

We studied the electronic properties of cupricite CuFe2S3 using X-ray emission and absorption spectroscopies to advance our understanding of this complicated orbital-crossing system.  Our analysis shows that the high-spin configuration in this compound is inaccurate, based on the results of our experiments and calculations.  In fact, there is significant mixing of the d-orbital waves in this material, which is in line with the Kugel-Bose model of exchange-driven instability.  Our findings also indicate that the spiral magnetic order in this compound results from the competition between the direct and antiferromagnetic interactions between the adjacent iron and copper ions.  Therefore, we propose that the exchange-driven instability gives this compound's orbital system its unique, intricate characteristics.

In combined quantum systems of light and matter, like cavity quantum electrodynamics, dynamic interactions between particles can result in linked oscillations between two or more states. This phenomenon, known as Rabi oscillation, is typically triggered by an external magnetic field. Researchers have recently discovered that in certain systems of photoexcited molecules within a solid, extremely large Rabi oscillations can occur without the need for an external magnetic field. These findings open up the possibility of developing more intricate quantum applications using this technique, potentially enabling the creation of complex quantum states and efficient light-matter interactions. These novel properties could also facilitate the development of efficient light-sensing technologies and optical data storage systems. Further study is required to fully explore the advantages of these discoveries.

Our investigation reveals that in a 2D lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper structure, closely spaced atomic layers host exceptional, adjustable Dirac points within a specific area of reduced symmetry. 

We have mathematically proven that these unique points, located at the center of irreducible wedges, possess the characteristics of exact, isolated, and stable Dirac points for both positive and negative energies. 

The unique feature of these points is their responsiveness to external pressure, where applying tension perpendicular to the lattice plane can shift the points from the center of a wedge to the edge, resulting in the formation of a ring-shaped, zero-carrier-belt in the energy spectrum. 

We have also found that applying shear strain to the lattice converts the discrete Dirac points into quasi-periodic, spiral-shaped gaps in the energy spectrum, opening up the possibility of adjusting the frequency of edge states along the Fermi ribs. 

These breakthroughs offer promising avenues for adjusting the electronic properties of the material through strain, potentially enabling the seamless integration of Dirac materials in flexible electronics.

Quantum states known as single-photon facilitated coherent states can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using the following process: a coherent state and an optical parametric oscillator state interact in a resonant cavity with the assistance of a single-photon detection device. We demonstrate that this facilitated state can be created through quantum-optical catalysis with respect to the coherent state's amplitude and the oscillator state's photon number, even in cases where the single-photon detection device fails or provides incorrect feedback. We also establish that the success of this facilitation depends on the failure probability of the single-photon detector and the quantum entanglement between the catalytic photon and the system, which can be maximized by adjusting the coherent state's amplitude and the oscillator state's photon number. Furthermore, we find that quantum-optical catalysis converts an arbitrary number of photons in the oscillator state into an exact number of photons in the single-photon facilitated coherent state.

In General Relativity, the use of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose framework simplifies complex tensor calculations, making them more manageable. This review article discusses the benefits of this approach by explaining the relationship between bivectors and tensors, illustrating how complex algebraic manipulations can be bypassed to derive significant geometric interpretations. Additionally, we establish the connection between the Weyl tensor's descriptive components and the bivector-based Newman-Penrose coefficients. By doing so, we demonstrate how the abstract algebraic properties of bivectors can be applied to interpret physical phenomena, such as electromagnetic field patterns, within the framework of General Relativity.

In recent years, various studies have successfully applied machine learning algorithms to predict material properties, yet similar successes with computer-aided design for polymers have proved elusive. This challenge is particularly difficult due to the unpredictable nature of polymer structures and property relationships. In our research, we propose a unique three-pronged approach, combining machine learning, computational chemistry, and optimization techniques to overcome these obstacles. Firstly, we utilize linear regression algorithms to establish correlations between polymer properties and atomic descriptors, breaking down complex molecules into manageable components. Secondly, we leverage the benefits of systematic variation in small fragments of the structure to our advantage. In doing so, we develop the PolyBuild framework, capable of efficiently designing polymers with desired electrical properties in the context of organic electronic applications.

Optimizing the performance of control systems under changing conditions can be achieved through the use of direct transcription methods. By converting the continuous control system into a discrete problem using sampling points, this approach can effectively tackle systems with complex nonlinear dynamics and constraints. The method involves generating an optimal trajectory for the system by dividing the time frame into segments and using interpolation. The tutorial will provide a step-by-step explanation of the algorithm, starting with a simplified example before moving on to a more complex scenario. The second example is based on a real-world problem. During the COVID-19 pandemic, ventilator shortages highlighted the need for safe dual-patient breathing assistance. To address this, we explored the possibility of modifying a single-patient ventilator to support two patients sharing the same device. The resulting control system was highly nonlinear and subject to severe constraints. We successfully demonstrated the applicability of the direct transcription method in this context, achieving a 20 to 30% improvement in system performance.

In this study, a complex medical condition, esophageal cancer, continues to pose a significant threat to global health.  Although esophageal cancer can be treated effectively with surgery and chemotherapy if detected early, its late stages often result in high mortality rates.  One reliable early detection method involves analyzing CT scan images of the esophagus.  However, accurately identifying tumors in these images proves challenging even for experienced radiologists.  To address this difficulty, researchers have been developing and testing automated cancer-detecting systems, particularly in the form of Deep Learning (DL) models.  In response to previous studies on cancer detection using DL models, we have developed a novel Densely Attentive Dense Unet (DDAUnet) framework that combines innovative dense and attention mechanisms to enhance the performance of tumor segmentation tasks.  To train this model, we utilized a large dataset of CT scan images and evaluated its efficacy compared to state-of-the-art competitors by executing repeated experiments at different sensitivity specificity balance points.  The DDAUnent outperformed all existing benchmark models in multiple experiments, demonstrating its potential as a reliable tool for automated esophageal cancer detection.

The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these locations typically have more geologically complex structures, making it crucial to implement real-time geosteering. This process involves continuously updating well plans based on the analysis of formation properties and dynamics during and even after drilling. This can be achieved through the efficient use of logging while drilling (LWD) data, which enables optimal placement of the well within the target formation. A potential challenge in this process is the interpretation of LWD data, which requires the integration of technical and geological expertise. This can be resolved by training a neural network to automatically classify LWD logs, reducing the need for continuous expert presence and allowing for the seamless integration of artificial intelligence in the drilling and geosteering process. Additionally, the incorporation of uncertainty measures into the classification algorithm can identify areas of uncertainty, further enhancing real-time decision making.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on identifying entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by introducing a new parsing algorithm that addresses nested NER in its entirety, allowing the recognition of both single and nested entities in a single step. Compared to traditional approaches, this method simultaneously achieves better performance on both individual and nested entity recognition tasks.

We present a counting method for bitangents to a rational surface quartic, which is based on tropical geometry. This approach allows us to count bitangents in time that scales linearly with the number of components in the dual tree. As a result, our method enables us to determine the rationality of the count for these bitangents and compute the count $\mathbb{A}^1$-homologically. Additionally, we can calculate the count of bitangents with signs, which gives us the real signed count of these bitangents.

The accuracy of wireless local area networking (WLAN) and Bluetooth (BT) location estimation is significantly impacted by external interference, which can mislead victims by presenting false WLAN and BT signals as artificial sources. This research investigates the adverse effects of such interference on location finding and proposes a novel method to enhance precision. Firstly, we establish that a circle of a specific radius, centered around the attacker, location accuracy significantly degrades to a maximum radius of 25 meters in an urban setting. Secondly, we develop and evaluate a circle-removal approach that eliminates the impact of the ring-shaped area of inaccuracy. Specifically, we adopt a metric called wall-crossing probability and control the standard deviation of BT samples to eliminate the effect of interference, ultimately achieving a location precision of 10 meters in urban environments.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective code switching and allowing them to express themselves freely in various languages through code mixing. As a result of this capability, code mixing offers a richer data source for extracting valuable information, complementing code sole (monolingual data in one language) and enabling NLP applications to reach a broader audience. Nonetheless, NLP systems face considerable difficulties in processing code mixing due to its diverse characteristics, including numerous scripts, different languages, and varied writing systems. System performance is further complicated by the absence of standard encoding, which makes data preprocessing challenging. To date, most NLP systems have exclusively focused on code sole, thereby neglecting the vast potential of code mixing. Developing models that can seamlessly handle multiple languages, scripts, and writing systems while being indifferent to standard encoding is crucial to leveraging code mixing data. This paper outlines existing work on code mixing, detailing current challenges, models, and preprocessing methods. Additionally, it provides an overview of code mixing applications, datasets, and evaluation metrics, which are primarily adapted from existing monolingual sources.

In recent years, significant advancements in learning-based methods for image description have been observed, offering promising results in modeling the alignment between images and their corresponding captions. However, the risk of over-reliance on these models for applications such as visually-assisted search and description of images with text has not been adequately addressed. One crucial aspect in developing robust practical solutions is the accurate evaluation of image description models, which is the primary focus of our study. We introduce a new evaluation framework that leverages human reference descriptions in relation to the descriptions generated by models, enabling the assessment of their performance. This framework allows for the consideration of various reference descriptions as equally valid, instead of treating one reference description as the sole ground truth. Our experimental results using the proposed framework provide valuable insights into the current state of image description models, and highlight the importance of incorporating diverse reference descriptions in the evaluation process.

Tantalum oxide, with the composition Ta$_2$O$_5$, has been extensively used in electronics due to its high dielectric properties.  Despite being widely applied, there is a fundamental issue that has not been resolved and requires attention - the lack of information about the crystal base structure.  Ta$_2$O$_5$ has been described in the literature by multiple authors using various phrases such as monocrystalline, polycrystalline, single layer, and island models.  Recent studies employed empirical methods to determine the structure, but these methods introduce their own assumptions and do not account for the system's dynamics.  To overcome this limitation, we have utilized the first-principles approach in the VASP program to explore different possible structures and then compared them using the Monte Carlo method in the CASTEP program.  Our results led us to identify one potential low-energy state, which we describe in detail, and found it to be resistant to lattice variations.  Conversely, the high-energy state we found became unstable under even minor changes in the lattice dimensions.  Notably, when comparing our findings to the experimental data collected by X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy, we observed some discrepancies, which led us to the conclusion that Ta$_2$O$_5$ films are prone to the effect of annealing temperature. The concept of the Big Sort refers to the significant separation of like-minded individuals into distinct social groups. These groups are often based on geographical locations that share similar political views. This study  examines the impact of the Big Sort on the spread of misinformation by analyzing user interactions on Reddit in the 2016 US election period. The study's findings show that the Big Sort has a minimal effect on promoting the dissemination of misinformation. Additionally, both areas with little sorting and heavily sorted areas demonstrate similar susceptibility to spreading misinformation. The study's data suggests that individual personality factors such as cognitive openness play a more significant role in influencing the spread of misinformation than do geographical sorting patterns.

We introduce a real-time detection system that flags potentially misleading information emerging rapidly from various digital sources, specifically focusing on identifying fake news events, suspicious transactions, and anomalous system behaviors. This system leverages a flexible and modular design, combining techniques such as natural language processing, machine learning, and correlation detection to detect irregularities at incredible speeds of up to 100,000 events per second. Our approach has resulted in the development of several successful applications, including a system that detected and prevented a security vulnerability attack and a tool that identified in-time and out-of-time anomalies in software system operations.

Instructors use speech to guide students, whether those students are humans or machines, in achieving tasks. Although the benefits of human-in-the-loop control for improving learning in robots are well-documented, the potential of human-in-the-loop learning for itself remains largely unexplored. This study examines speech used to teach robots to perform tasks by observing their actions, by looking at how acoustic features change in response to the detection of errors and the completion of subtasks. Two aspects of speech were found to be particularly significant in this context: tempo and the spectrum. When a subtask is identified, speech accelerates and takes on a more vibrant quality, characteristic of excitement, while detection of an error causes speech to slow and become more subdued. These findings are validated through multiple methods, including the application of control systems and the verification of multiple interpretations of data. They provide the foundation for developing learning systems that can accurately interpret the speech of human instructors, and ultimately use this interpretation to adjust their own performance.

Building on previous work, we propose a novel approach to generating random trees of any degree, based on a unique ordering of the nodes as they are connected. This ordering, which we call "connection order," enables us to construct trees systemically. Our method produces trees with the desired distribution, even those with degree sequences that don't form a valid graph. Furthermore, this approach extends beyond trees to random graphs with a specific degree sequence, allowing us to generate graphs efficiently using a sampling process that leverages the unique connection order of the nodes.

Certain powerful mathematical theories including geometric mechanics and fluid dynamics rely heavily on the use of Euler-Arnold equations and their extensions. These foundational theories then establish the framework for conformal field theories to operate within this broader context. This paper aims to explore the underlying principles that make conformal field theories so complex, with a focus on identifying the essential characteristics of these theories. It is essential to note that this study is performed for theories living in high-dimensional spacetimes.

The growing presence of conversational bots in daily life demands a more effective testing methodology. Unlike traditional software testing, machine testing addresses this need by leveraging a different approach. To achieve this, we've developed a machine learning model that generates varied test cases, allowing for more comprehensive testing of bots. In this workshop, we'll not only explore the principles of machine testing but also demonstrate the potential of data-driven methods in this field, building on top of our previous research.

Using a sophisticated mathematical model known as the Moshkovitz-VanderKoijs formalism, we re-examined the gravitational impact of an undiscovered planet on the movement of the other planets in our solar system, specifically focusing on Jupiter and Saturn. By tweaking various orbital parameters of the hidden world, we found that its influence could potentially counteract the effects of general relativity, thus affecting the alignment of the two largest planets. Notably, we discovered that the most distinctive signature of the hidden planet on the motion of the other planets occurs when it is located at a significant distance from them, primarily due to the overwhelming dominance of Newton's gravitational force over any other force. As a result, we found that the most distinctive effect of the hidden planet on Jupiter is a minimal 0.0003 degrees of variation in the position of the planet during a specific phase of its orbit, which is below the level of precision in the measurements. To provide some context, the average error in tracking the movement of the planet is about 0.0005 degrees, also known as an arcsecond. Despite being statistically insignificant, we believe that future, more precise measurements could potentially reveal the existence of the hidden planet.

In the context of neural machine translation and interpretation, the proposed Neural Machine Interpretation (NMI) model builds upon the translation archive framework. The translation archive is a knowledge base that contains previously generated sentence pairs and their corresponding translations. By incorporating this knowledge, the NMI model can leverage the stored knowledge to improve its understanding and generate more accurate interpretations. In our approach, the NMI model utilizes the translation archive in a monolingual manner, enabling it to learn about the target language by exploiting the available sentence translations. When producing interpretations, the model can select source-target language pairs from the archive that match the input text, thereby producing more coherent and meaningful outputs. Our results demonstrate that the NMI model can effectively utilize the translation archive to generate high-quality interpretations on various topics, even with limited training data.

Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, which are referred to as Conformal Cyclic Cosmology markers, could provide evidence for the theory of Conformal Cyclic Cosmology. These patterns would originate from an earlier universe contraction phase and correspond to areas where the universe's structure is repeating in a cyclical pattern. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP CMB data to search for the predicted anomalies, specifically looking at alignments, circular patterns, and geometric shapes. Our analysis used a statistical testing method to evaluate the likelihood of these features occurring naturally, and the results showed that the anomalies we were looking for are highly unlikely to occur by chance. Furthermore, our findings suggested that the features we were searching for are not unique and are therefore not specific to Conformal Cyclic Cosmology.

This paper builds upon previous work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which involved introducing an Yamabe flow based on fractional curvature and demonstrating the existence of mild solutions. The current research expands on that study by establishing the convergence of the flow under certain data conditions within the L^{\frac{n+4}{n-2}} norm. The new approach utilizes a more detailed analysis of the fractional Yamabe flow and proves key bounds within the specified norm, ultimately leading to the convergence of solutions given those conditions are met.

Prototypes have been widely used in machine learning due to their balance of computational efficiency and effective data representation.  Moreover, learning prototypes that represent the overall characteristics of a class can significantly simplify the classification process by minimizing the need for exhaustive nearest neighbor search.  This work proposes an approach to learn class-specific prototypes from data, even with small data sets.  To efficiently utilize the limited data, a prototype is represented by multiple exemplars, reducing the dimensionality from data points.  To further improve classification performance with small data sets, this work also introduces the use of neighbor graphs between data points.  By leveraging the intrinsic structure within the data, more accurate prototypes can be learned.  Moreover, this work develops an efficient algorithm to learn the prototypes, batch-wise from the data.  The proposed approach is evaluated and compared with existing methods on multiple datasets, resulting in state-of-the-art performance in particular scenarios.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) that leverages multiple domains even in the presence of extreme sparsity. In MSDCR, we develop an Enhanced Comprehensive Attribute Preference Learning (ECAPL) model to capture a comprehensive understanding of user preferences across all domains, incorporating both explicit behavior data and latent attribute preferences. Furthermore, we propose a Multi-Domain ECAPL (MDECAPL) framework, which includes a cooperative ECAPL component and a model selection strategy to handle the diverse characteristics of varying domains. To tackle the challenges of high-dimensional rating data, MSDCR employs a novel Sparse Reverse Propagation (SRP) technique. We evaluate MSDCR on four real-world datasets, demonstrating its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art CDR methods.

Convex optimization issues often incorporate conic representations that leverage a wide variety of convex cones to advertise problem structure.  Despite the broad applicability of conic formulations, there is a limited selection of solvers globally capable of handling all commonly used cones.  To complement existing solver options, this paper introduces the Hypatia function for conic optimization problems, capable of automatically converting any expression involving these cones into a form amenable to solution by CBC or COUENNE.  The paper also presents results of benchmark tests comparing the three available solution strategies, including direct formulation, graph-based heuristics, and a hybrid of both.

The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality assessment to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially in research and clinical settings. Several approaches have been explored to develop MRI quality evaluation methods, but none have been consistently effective due to the complex nature of image evaluation, which goes beyond mere technical aspects. Essentially, evaluating MRI quality involves a combination of technical, expert, and contextual factors, including previous experiences, expectations, and assumptions that cannot be captured through mere model predictions. These underlying variables influence the formation of a general understanding of MRI quality, making it challenging to develop a universally applicable definition. Consequently, any proposed solution must tackle this multi-dimensional generalization problem, involving both the development of a comprehensive definition of MRI quality and a universally acceptable evaluation standards.

The rising number of privately owned electric vehicles is causing concern about the resilience of urban distribution networks. To address this issue, we propose an innovative three-tier agent system to optimize the functioning of private electric vehicle chargers in conjunction with the distribution network. The system includes a network agent that facilitates decentralized decision-making and optimizes network performance, as well as private agent chargers that make decisions based on their own objectives, likely prioritizing private convenience over network needs. To manage potential conflicts, we develop a multi-objective co-evolutionary algorithm to find solutions that balance the needs of both the network and the private vehicles. Our results show that collaborating between network agents and private vehicles can lead to more resilient and efficient networks, while those vehicles still derive benefits from the relationship.

Intel's Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (DC PMM) offers a persistent storage capability, enabling applications to access data with both extreme low latency and high throughput. To effectively utilize its features, software must be optimized for Optane's characteristics, which vary depending on data access patterns. This assessment explores Optane's performance in different scenarios, including benchmark tests, real-world workloads, and microbenchmarks, to gauge its behavior in various contexts. Key findings include Optane's exceptional results in tests benefiting from persistent storage, such as Hadoop and Kafka, as well as situations where its performance is comparable to DRAM, like simple scalar operations. However, in cases where data is accessed randomly or in clusters, such as database queries, Optane may perform worse than expected, presenting opportunities for optimization across the system software stack.

In collaborative scenarios involving periodic tasks, agents are motivated to meet at optimal intervals that balance the frequency and duration of their meetings. This study introduces a model representing these meetings as overlapping periods with fixed lengths, subject to capacity constraints. The paper aims to determine the optimal meeting frequency and timing for each agent, given exogenous arrival and departure times, within a fixed planning horizon. To solve this problem, a discrete drive-based incentive mechanism is developed, effectively dividing the planning horizon into several optimal meeting windows. The mechanism's performance is evaluated in two scenarios: when the planning horizon is divided evenly among all agents, and when it is dominated by one or two agents. The study provides computational results analyzing the drive-based incentive mechanism's efficiency and contrast its performance with a random approach. The proposed solution can be implemented using a multi-agent system, providing a flexible framework for solving this type of problem.

We examined the structure, electronic properties, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using the Coherent Potential Method and Density Functional Theory. Our calculations showed that CmSn3 has a hexagonal Ni2Sn3 structure, while GdSn3 and the GdxCm1-xSn3 series adopt a monoclinic Au2Mn3 structure. We found that CmSn3 exhibits a metallic state with magnetic characteristics and a lattice parameter that matches reported values. In contrast, the band structure of GdSn3 reveals a metal-to-semiconductor transition with increasing spin-orbit coupling, while the band gap in CmSn3 is minimal. A magnetic state is observed in both CmSn3 and GdSn3. Within the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, increasing Gd content leads to a shorter lattice parameter, a larger magnetic moment, and a transition from a semiconductor to a metallic state. These predictions align with experimental findings for the Au2Mn3 phase and offer a theoretical framework for understanding the magnetic properties of these compounds.

Lattice QCD calculations allow for the prediction of masses of exotic, multi-quark particles, such as baryons and mesons, which are responsible for the fundamental force of nature known as the strong interaction. By applying the lattice method to QCD, researchers can accurately calculate the masses of these particles, independent of theoretical models. In this study, we provide a detailed explanation of the lattice method used to calculate the masses of exotic baryons and mesons, while also highlighting the advantages of this approach over other methods. We also review the current state of predictions made using the lattice method and discuss the role of form factors in these predictions. Furthermore, we outline the expectations of future developments in this field.

Building upon the foundation theorem of intergrated polynomials from M. Hohmann and A. Prester, relating the central cover of an algebra to its nilpotent part, this paper generalizes this concept to the finite irreducible complex reflection groups known as Coxeter groups of the B-type, specifically those with rank greater than one.

The influence of weak gravitational lensing on Type Ia supernovae observations is expected to be minimal, especially since the density field around these events is typically low. We utilize the Pantheon sample to distinguish between a lensing effect and other explanations for the apparent divergence in local and distant Type Ia supernovae. Assuming a standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, we find the amount of lensing required to explain the observed divergence would be greater than expected based on field statistics. In fact, this excess is so significant that it could counter the suppression of nearby Type Ia supernovae, leading to a wrong conclusion about the Hubble constant if lensing is ignored. Our analysis also reveals that lensing has a different impact on supernovae with blue and red spectra, a distinction that could be a lensing effect if it holds in larger samples.

These are lecture notes for a 6-hour mini-course presented at the University of Oxford in April-May 2022, as part of the Isaac Newton Institute's programme 'Stochastic Partial Differential Equations'. These notes are intended for graduate students and early-career researchers, assuming a basic understanding of probability, real analysis, and PDEs. They provide an in-depth introduction to the world of stochastic PDEs, starting with the underlying principles of stochastic analysis, before delving into more advanced topics in SPDEs.

In photonic integrated systems, where space is limited, the efficient conversion between different types of waveguide interactions is crucial for ultimate design performance. Through a novel point-like connection, the conversion between lateral tension and transverse interactions is achieved with minimal size requirements. By utilizing the SOI process, we were able to create a 'T hub' that facilitates a highly efficient conversion from lateral tension to the lossless imaginary interaction, thus enabling the seamless transfer of signal from one type to another.

The objective of this study is to contrast automatic image analysis methods, specifically
histogram-based segmentation, radon transform-based segmentation, and deep learning
approaches, for effectively identifying tumors in MRI images.

In this research, we present an algebraic approach to identifying degenerate and non-degenerate minima of the Kac-Wallis distribution, initially established in [AWZ19], [Jang19]. Our method yields a novel criterion for determining the minimum of this distribution, along with a corresponding algebraic formula for the minimum value. This, in turn, enables the identification of degenerate minima, which may not be found using the geometric method presented in [AWZ19]. Building upon this foundation, we also explore minimum values of the Kac-Wallis distribution with specific parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$, expressing these values as sums of powers of the underlying field F_q. Additionally, we establish connections between these minimum values and specific polynomials within the Witt ring of F_q, particularly the 2-Sato-Tate group and its associated polynomial.

The problem of stellar activity noise in spectroscopic planetary searches can be addressed through the removal of chromospheric lines from the analysis. However, identifying and excluding all such lines is impractical due to the large number involved, especially with the increasing availability of high-resolution stellar spectra. This study compares two approaches to automatically remove lines associated with stellar activity from the analysis of exoplanet searches using the least-squares deconvolution method. The first approach, based on line parameters such as wavelength and strength, and the second approach, involving randomized line selection, are assessed for their effectiveness in recovering mock planetary signals in the presence of stellar activity and noise typical of the ESPADON algorithm. The results show that while both methods yield comparable performance in terms of recovery of planetary periods, the randomized line selection approach outperforms the parametric method in recovering the masses of the planets.

On-demand data collection is a crucial operation in Wireless Sensor Networks, specifically the gathering phase can be inefficient due to unclear inter-node connections and varying distances between nodes. To tackle this issue, we present two techniques to enhance the performance of this stage: Hierarchical Scope Sectoring and Bidirectional Link Caliber Estimation. Our methods divide the area of interest into segmented regions based on the distance between nodes and create defined areas around each node by calculating the appropriate sector size, thereby reducing unnecessary data transmission. Additionally, our approach includes estimating the quality of links between nodes to select the most effective path for data collection, ultimately resulting in a better overall performance. Simulation results show that our techniques yield significant improvements in energy efficiency, network lifetime, and total collected data.

When evaluating the performance of object recognition models, context is typically ignored, with images being assessed in isolation. Yet, context has been observed to significantly impact both human perception and the behavior of machine learning algorithms. This study aims to understand the role of context in object recognition, considering both explicit and implicit aspects. To this end, a novel framework is introduced that enables the assessment of context for machine learning models, including those with deep neural network architecture. The framework's effectiveness is then demonstrated through a practical application involving the evaluation of a machine learning model's performance under varying context conditions. Furthermore, our study reveals that context has a substantial impact on object recognition, with variables influencing the recognition process including the distribution of objects within an image, the presence of additional images, and the context provided by an image's semantic description.

The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are related to the Trudinger-Moser inequality, which involves singular weights. The system in question has nonhomogeneous coefficients, making it a nonstandard problem. The authors leverage a type of concavity approach, along with the Moser-Trudinger inequality under certain constraints, to obtain multiple solution criteria for the system in question. The concavity method is a key tool in their proof. The paper also provides an existence and uniqueness theorem for a related Kirchhoff type equation. The results obtained in this paper can be seen as an extension of earlier work on the Trudinger-Moser inequality to a more complicated elliptic system of equations.

We establish concentration inequalities for sums of dependent binary random variables, where the dependency follows a specific 'anti-correlated' pattern. Specifically, let's consider $X_i$, independent and identically distributed random variables that take values $0$ or $1$, with $p$ being the probability of $X_i$ equaling $1$. Also, assume there's a constant $c \in [0,1]$ such that for any two subsets of these variables, the expected product of their values is less than or equal to $p^2(1-c)$. We demonstrate that with probability at least $1-\alpha$, the absolute difference between the number of variables equal to $1$ and expected value is less than or equal to $cp^{-1}\sqrt{\log(2/\alpha)\sum_{i}X_i}+cp^{-1}\sqrt{\log(2/\alpha)}$. This achievement generalizes previous results from Bopanna, Easley, and Kahn ('Anti-Correlated Binary Variables and Concentration Inequalities', 2020) by removing the restriction on correlated variables and the condition that the correlation be strong, thereby providing new insights into the properties of highly uncorrelated binary variables.

Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic greater than two, and consider the ring of power series $R$ over the Witt vectors of $k$, expanded in variables $t_1, \dots, t_d$. The main aim of this study is to generalize classical Fontaine-Messing theory to a base ring of the form $R$. To accomplish this, we establish key results, including the existence of a category of six-dimensional crystalline $t$-divided $R$-modules with an absolute Gelfand-MacPherson genus, and demonstrate that this genus serves as a measure of the dimension of the associated crystalline module. Additionally, we show that a specific class of $R$-modules, namely those obtained from finite free $W(k)$-modules via the Fontaine-Messing construction, possess an integral property linked to the genus of these modules. This property is demonstrated to be a variant of what might be described as 'Fontaine-Messing divisibility'.

This study explores the difference in dihadron production between helicity and transverse momentum distributions in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering, specifically focusing on the correlation between the helicity of the observed hadron and the lepton. We discovered that the deviation in the cosine distribution of the observed hadron's helicity is significant across various $k_T$ scales, ranging from 5 times smaller to 5 times larger than the average $k_T$ value. This finding reveals that the $k_T$ movement is not the primary factor in dihadron production and suggests that the observed hadron's motion is influenced by the spin of the struck quark. We found that the cosine deviation in the helicity distribution is more pronounced when the observed hadron is moving in the same direction as the lepton, while in the opposite case, the deviation is less pronounced and may be related to the chiral nature of the quark's spin.

In the context of an infinite square well potential, we calculate the energy shift of Fock's state as an expectation value in both the classical and quantum frameworks, confirming that their results coincide. Furthermore, by applying this energy shift to a massive particle in a one-dimensional de Sitter space using quantum field theory, we derive the associated potential energy for Fock's state and demonstrate that it mirrors the energy shift calculated through the infinite square well model.

We have reworked and simplified the proof of a key theorem from Alpern--Leroy's work involving symplectic alterations in the context of weakly equivalent rings. Additionally, we have expanded upon this concept for weakly equivalent schemes within the framework of algebraic geometry.

This paper presents a new approach to suggesting entities on a knowledge graph based on user input, using a layered graph representation that leverages Wikipedia content. The entity suggestion feature was part of the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, a web entity search platform that provided detailed information for over a billion entities. However, this feature had a significant limitation - it only suggested exact matches from the index. To overcome this, we developed an entity suggestion approach that used a layered graph representation, incorporating Wikipedia content to provide suggestions. This approach involved building a knowledge graph layer that combined entity descriptions from Wikipedia with corresponding concept layers. We used this combined graph for entity suggestion, targeting topics that were not fully represented. The results showed a significant improvement in covering more topics and entity descriptions. This approach led to a more engaging user experience, covering 25.3% more topics with just five entity suggestions.
